title: Java: the language (topics 01-16)
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 fund-java-language row). Scope = Fundamentals Java topic gates 01-16. The binding list has 13 rows and the cap is 12: '== vs equals, the Integer cache' (topic 01) and 'equals/hashCode/compareTo must agree' (topic 08) are one equality idea. Topics 05, 09 and 16 have no row of their own. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: == on objects compares references, which only looks right for small cached Integers; equals, hashCode and compareTo must agree on the same fields.
ideas.why: Code that compares boxed numbers with == passes tests with small values and fails in production, and inconsistent equality makes sets and maps lose or duplicate entries.
ideas.prompt: `Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b` is true, but the same check with 1000 is false. Separately, a TreeSet of versions that already holds '1.0' refuses to add '1.0.0' although equals says they differ. Explain both.
ideas.answer: Boxing reuses cached Integer objects for -128 to 127, so == finds the same object for 127 but two different objects for 1000; compare values with equals or unbox. A TreeSet decides duplicates with compareTo, not equals, so a comparator that calls the two versions equal must agree with equals and hashCode, or sorted and hashed collections behave differently.

ideas.idea: Strings never change; every concatenation makes a new string, so build text in a loop with StringBuilder or String.join.
ideas.why: Concatenating inside a loop copies the growing string each time, which turns a linear job quadratic on large inputs.
ideas.prompt: A CSV exporter builds each file with `out += row + "\n"` over 200,000 rows and takes minutes. A colleague suspects the disk. What do you suspect, and why?
ideas.answer: Each += creates a new String and copies everything built so far, so the total copying grows with the square of the row count. Append to one StringBuilder (or write rows straight to a Writer) and convert once at the end. The disk is not the problem; the repeated copying is.

ideas.idea: Model a closed set of cases as an enum or a sealed interface and let the compiler check coverage: an enum switch expression with no default must name every constant.
ideas.why: A default branch silently accepts new cases, so adding a subtype or constant compiles and then does the wrong thing at runtime.
ideas.prompt: Shipping options are an enum with a switch statement and a default that returns the standard price. A new EXPRESS option ships at the standard price. How would a switch expression have helped?
ideas.answer: A switch expression must be exhaustive, so with one arm per constant and no default, adding EXPRESS fails to compile until someone decides its price. A default hides that decision. For a sealed interface on Java 17, switch patterns are not standard yet (they are in 21), so put the price in a method each permitted type must implement.

ideas.idea: Use records for immutable data carriers with value equality, and enums for a fixed set of states that can carry behaviour such as allowed transitions.
ideas.why: Hand-written data classes drift (a field missing from equals), and states kept as strings accept typos and illegal transitions.
ideas.prompt: Order status is a String field, and services check `status.equals("SHIPED")` in places. An audit finds orders that went from CANCELLED back to PAID. How do records and enums fix this design?
ideas.answer: Make status an enum, so a misspelled state does not compile, and give it the transition rule, for example a method that says which next states are allowed, so every service asks the same place. Carry the order's data in a record, whose equals, hashCode and toString come from its components and cannot drift.

ideas.idea: Producer extends, consumer super: read from a List<? extends T>, write into a List<? super T>; generic types are erased at runtime, so List<String> and List<Integer> are one class.
ideas.why: Without PECS, utility methods accept too little and force casts; without knowing erasure, people expect instanceof or overloads to tell generic types apart.
ideas.prompt: `static void copy(List<Number> src, List<Number> dst)` cannot be called with a List<Integer> source or a List<Object> destination. Fix the signature and explain what the wildcards allow.
ideas.answer: `static <T> void copy(List<? extends T> src, List<? super T> dst)`. The source only produces values, so any list of a subtype works; the destination only consumes them, so any list of a supertype works. Note that at runtime both are plain List, so the method cannot check the element type itself.

ideas.idea: Pick the collection by how it is used (lookup, order, uniqueness, queueing); iterators fail fast when the collection changes under them except through the iterator itself.
ideas.why: A list used for lookups makes every check a scan, and removing from a collection inside its for-each throws ConcurrentModificationException.
ideas.prompt: A job removes expired sessions with `for (Session s : sessions) if (s.expired()) sessions.remove(s);` and crashes with ConcurrentModificationException. It also checks `sessions.contains(id)` thousands of times a second on an ArrayList. Fix both.
ideas.answer: Remove through the iterator or with sessions.removeIf(Session::expired), which changes the list without invalidating the loop. For frequent membership checks keep the sessions in a HashMap or HashSet keyed by id, so lookups are constant time instead of a scan of the whole list.

ideas.idea: Streams are lazy and single-use: nothing runs until a terminal operation, each stream can be consumed once, and lambdas inside should not change outside state.
ideas.why: Reusing a stream throws IllegalStateException, and side effects in map or peek make results depend on evaluation order and parallelism.
ideas.prompt: A report builds `Stream<Order> paid = orders.stream().filter(Order::isPaid)` once, then calls paid.count() and paid.mapToLong(...).sum(). It also adds to an outer list inside map(). Find the bugs.
ideas.answer: The second terminal operation fails because a stream can be consumed only once; keep a Supplier or a collected list and stream it again. Adding to an outer list inside map is a side effect that may run in any order or not at all; collect the result with a collector instead.

ideas.idea: Use Optional only as a return type that says 'maybe absent', and consume it with map, flatMap, orElse or orElseThrow, never with a bare get().
ideas.why: Optional fields and parameters add allocation and nulls of their own, and get() without a check is just a NullPointerException with a new name.
ideas.prompt: `Optional<Employee> m = find(id); return m.get().getManager().getEmail();` throws NoSuchElementException and sometimes NullPointerException. Rewrite it in the intended Optional style.
ideas.answer: Chain the steps that may be missing: `find(id).map(Employee::getManager).map(Manager::getEmail)`, then decide once at the end with orElse, orElseGet or orElseThrow and a clear message. If getManager can be absent, return Optional from it and use flatMap. get() without a check gives up the protection Optional exists for.

ideas.idea: Open anything closeable with try-with-resources: it closes in reverse order on every path and keeps a failure during close as a suppressed exception.
ideas.why: Hand-written finally blocks leak handles on early returns, and an exception thrown while closing can replace the original error you needed.
ideas.prompt: A reader throws while parsing, and then its close() throws too. In the old finally-based code the log only shows the close error. What does try-with-resources do differently?
ideas.answer: The parsing exception stays the primary one, and the exception from close() is attached to it as a suppressed exception (getSuppressed), so both reach the log. Resources are closed automatically in reverse order of opening, on normal exit and on exceptions alike.

ideas.idea: Store and compare moments as Instant in UTC, apply a ZoneId only at the edges where people see or enter local times, and do calendar arithmetic in that zone.
ideas.why: Mixing local times and zones breaks billing dates, reminders and reports twice a year when clocks change and whenever users span time zones.
ideas.prompt: A reminder scheduler stores LocalDateTime values from users in different countries and fires them by comparing to LocalDateTime.now() on the server. Reminders fire hours early or late. What do you change?
ideas.answer: Turn the user's local date-time and zone into an Instant when the reminder is saved (ZonedDateTime.of(local, zone).toInstant()) and compare Instants with the server's clock. Convert back to the user's zone only for display. For 'every month on the 31st' style rules, do the arithmetic in the user's zone.

ideas.idea: Shared mutable state needs both visibility and atomicity (synchronized, locks, atomics or concurrent collections); executors must be shut down and awaited.
ideas.why: count++ from several threads loses updates, a flag written by one thread may never be seen by another, and a forgotten executor keeps the JVM alive.
ideas.prompt: A batch job counts words with 8 threads writing into one HashMap and a plain int total, then exits. Totals are off and sometimes the process never ends. Explain each symptom.
ideas.answer: HashMap and total++ are not thread-safe: concurrent read-modify-writes overwrite each other. Use ConcurrentHashMap.merge and a LongAdder, or give each thread its own map and combine them. The process hangs because the executor's threads are still alive; call shutdown() and awaitTermination() when the work is submitted.

ideas.idea: Compose CompletableFutures with thenCompose and thenCombine, give remote calls timeouts, and handle the exceptional path explicitly with exceptionally or handle.
ideas.why: Blocking get() calls throw away the concurrency, and an unhandled exceptional completion leaves a caller waiting or loses the error entirely.
ideas.prompt: A product page calls price, stock and reviews services by calling `.get()` on each future in turn. When reviews is down the page hangs for 30 seconds. Rewrite the flow.
ideas.answer: Start all three calls, combine them with thenCombine or allOf, and avoid blocking in the middle. Give the reviews call orTimeout or completeOnTimeout with a short deadline and an exceptionally fallback to no reviews, so the page renders without them instead of hanging. Decide per call which failures are fatal.
